The Air Force's announcement that it has "on-orbit space control weapons"
generated a flurry of identical articles, nearly all about potential war with
China and Russia. The coverage was bristling with Cold War-era defense-speak:
deterrence, stability, signaling.

The real reason for the announcement came a few sentences later in Air Force
Secretary Troy Meink's keynote at the Air, Space & Cyber Conference. It had
little to do with space weapons, which were never actually identified (but
I'll reveal them in a moment). It was about drumming up money.

"In today's rapidly changing threat environment, we cannot expect a world-
class military if we choose not to invest in it," Meink
[said](https://www.af.mil/News/Article-Display/Article/4600887/meink-offers-
blueprint-for-modernizing-air-space-forces-affordably/). "Many of the weapons,
components, or systems we have to buy have outrun the cost curve. They perform
extremely well, but the costs are growing faster than the rate of inflation."

He then [lamented](https://www.af.mil/News/Article-
Display/Article/4600887/meink-offers-blueprint-for-modernizing-air-space-
forces-affordably/): "Today, we face a mix of rapidly changing technologies …
and a budget process for a different pace of warfare."

Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess was even more blunt this week.

"In the coming years," he
[said](https://x.com/AFA_Air_Space/status/2099857959928902134?s=20), "we will
make disciplined and responsible choices about how we build and sustain our
combat advantage, which means scaling our ability to respond to threats." Then
he threw in: "We need your help, Congress."

Translation: money, money, money. Your money.

Today, by complete coincidence I'm sure, Space Force posted a
[new](https://www.spaceforce.mil/About-Us/Fact-Sheets/Fact-Sheet-
Display/Article/4297159/space-threat-fact-sheet/) "Space Threat Fact Sheet."
The Space Force wants you to know that what you've already given (over $100
billion) is not enough. So now they're asking for another $71.3 billion -- the
biggest one-year jump any military branch has gotten since 1952,
[according](https://csps.aerospace.org/sites/default/files/2026-08/Wilson_FY27BudgetBrief_20260817.pdf)
to the Aerospace Center for Space Policy and Strategy.

Space Force has some [spaceballs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceballs)!

If you think I'm being too cynical, Secretary Meink all but says it himself in
explaining why he announced the "new" space weapon at all.

"... at this point, we are trying to say that we also need capabilities to not
only defend the joint force from space-enabled attack, but defend our assets.
And so, I think it was time that within the Department of War we talked about
it, and it's time to talk about that we have the capabilities to make sure
that we can do what the joint force needs," Meink
[told](https://www.defenseone.com/threats/2026/09/orbit-weapons-space-force-
leader/415999/) Defense One (which, to its credit, also pointed out the
enormity of Space Force's budget request).

In other words: _show me the money!_

Down the hall from the keynote, STARCOM commander Maj. Gen. James E. Smith
[hammered](https://www.dvidshub.net/news/574674/starcom-highlights-plan-
deliver-space-force-growth) home the same message: "Predictable budget
resources will remain vital as we scale operations to maintain our FY27
momentum."

Don't you just love how they've now decided to say "scale" instead of
increase?

If you're wondering how the Pentagon managed to get what is essentially an
infomercial for more money into every major media outlet, take a look at the
Air Force's own write-up.

"Meink also acknowledged for the first time that Space Force has deployed
weapons in space," it says.

"For the first time" is irresistible to a journalism 1.0 reporter. Mainstream
media defines newsworthy as simply that which is "new" (I guess they just
dropped the "worthy" part).

The irony is that it was already pretty widely known that the U.S. military
has weapons in space.

* * *

"On-orbit space control weapons" sounds ominous, like the United States has
some photon torpedo of the future. The reality is a little more pedestrian and
a lot more routine than a screaming "news" story would suggest.

Every 90 minutes, a super-secret X-37B [mini-space
shuttle](https://www.boeing.com/features/2026/04/x-37b-keeps-pushing-the-edge-
of-on-orbit-testing) orbits the earth, a "weapon" in space that has been doing
so for the last 16 years. The one up there right now -- spaceplane 8 -- has
been orbiting since August 21 of last year. Round and round it goes, part of a
Top Secret "special access program" that's an open secret, but one where the
security goons have managed to keep the true purpose secret for more than a
decade.

When the spaceplane was first sent into orbit in 2010, it was decidedly
pointed downward, "testing" new hardware in real space environments, the
military said. It also harbored an even deeper secret: a "Rods from God"
weapon that would be able to attack any point on earth, literally a bundle of
steel penetrators that could arrive in seconds and from who knows where.

Rods from God is now an obsolete idea. Despite fake reports of the U.S.
[running out of weapons](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/the-pentagons-new-
missile-gap) because of the Iran war, it has more than enough rods to destroy
anything and everything on the planet.

In 16 years, though, the world has changed. China and Russia have developed
their own robust space capabilities and have deployed a variety of satellites
and payloads that can engage in "orbital warfare," as the military calls it.
War in space is now indeed _in space_ -- the focus being up there, where the
U.S. and allies have become ever more dependent on our own satellites. (Did
you know that the U.S. has more than 10,500 satellites in active orbit, more
than 90 percent of which are part of the SpaceX Starlink mega-constellation?)

The X-37B is not the only "on orbit" weapon, either, as satellites themselves
are now part of the space arsenal. Earlier this month, the military conducted
Apollo Maneuvers 26, an exercise practicing on-orbit maneuvers of satellites
to position them to conduct offensive operations to destroy enemy
communications, navigation, and spying capabilities. The military openly talks
about these "Rendezvous Proximity Operations." It is decidedly quiet about the
"weapons" themselves, whether they be electronic warfare jamming and spoofing
or other forms of cyberattack.

Meink also said that a U.S. space-based interceptor program had moved "from
initial contract to flight-ready hardware in less than one year," indicating
that something new was recently developed. It could be as simple as a ramming
satellite, but that is much too simple for the gold-plated developers.
Instead, military sources and documents tell me, it is more likely a "directed
energy" weapon, either a laser or high-power microwave, or something even more
exotic.

According to one contracting document I've obtained, the military laboratories
are still working on developing a "space-based neutral particle beam weapon,"
a Reagan-era Star Wars dream that manages to still suck tax dollars out of us
despite nothing to show for it. Again, directed energy is an open secret, but
the specifics of whatever space weapons exist are not only under "special
access programs," they are also part of "special technical operations" that
demand a different security clearance.

One military document describes the world of orbital warfare as "deception,
disruption, denial, degradation, and destruction." Many of those five D's take
place from earth. Space systems with code names like Bounty Hunter, Silent
Sentry, Falcons, Browns and Meadowlands have been generally described in
budget and other documents. Others, like the space-related Red Cloud
electronic warfare system, or the Red Dragon and Kraken cyberspace warfare
systems, have not been publicly acknowledged or explained.

The bottom line? The United States has a new space weapon, but the definition
of "weapon" is unclear -- and what's new is questionable. That's another
important distinction the media coverage missed. What is a weapon these days
often defies description. But the imperfect word still connotes a bomb or
missile, that is, launched from an airplane, ship or tank. Space indeed might
be the final frontier, but one reason the Spaceballs think they need more is
that so much already goes to old-fashioned hardware, built around a now
obsolete image of war.

Let's hope we don't end up shoveling an extra half-a-_trillion_ dollars into
the Pentagon money pit next year alone, as they've requested.

May the Schwartz be with you, Congress.
